identification.title: Take My Life and Let It Be
identification.notes: Written by Frances Ridley Havergal in 1874 after a night spent praying for the household she was staying in. Sung to several tunes, most often HENDON or NOTTINGHAM. Words and traditional tunes are public domain; some modern settings are not.

claims.structuralNotes: Six short verses in couplets, no chorus, each offering a different part of the singer's life in turn: life, hands, feet, voice, silver, will, heart. The form is a list, and the list is the argument.

claims.claim: The singer offers their whole life to God to be consecrated.
claims.subject: Consecration

claims.claim: The singer's hands, feet and voice are given over to God's use.
claims.subject: Consecration

claims.claim: The singer's money and possessions are surrendered without reservation.
claims.subject: Possessions

claims.claim: The singer's will is handed over to become God's.
claims.subject: The will

claims.claim: The singer's love and heart are poured out at God's feet.
claims.subject: Love for God

strengths.title: Names what is surrendered, item by item
strengths.explanation: Most songs of surrender offer 'everything' and specify nothing. This one hands over hands, feet, voice, money and will separately, so a congregation cannot sing it without noticing what they have just said about their bank account.
strengths.scriptureRationale: Present your bodies as a living sacrifice — a bodily, itemised offering rather than a sentiment.

strengths.title: The will surrendered, not just the actions
strengths.explanation: One verse gives over the singer's will to become God's. That is the hardest thing in the list and the hymn does not soften it or leave it out.
strengths.scriptureRationale: Not my will, but yours, be done — the surrender the verse asks for.

strengths.title: Money named directly
strengths.explanation: Silver and gold are handed over by name. Congregational song almost never mentions possessions, and a hymn that makes the room say it out loud is doing something unusual.
strengths.scriptureRationale: You cannot serve God and money — which is why naming it matters.

theological.assessment: A hymn of consecration that refuses to be vague. Where most songs offer everything and name nothing, this one hands over hands, feet, voice, money and will separately, so a congregation hears exactly what it has committed. The surrender of the will is not softened and the money is not skipped. What it never supplies is the ground: the offering is made without any statement of what God has done to make it fitting.

strengths.title: Short verses that can be selected
strengths.explanation: Six self-contained couplets mean a leader can use three or all six without breaking the argument. That flexibility is rare and practically useful.

strengths.title: Simple tunes, widely known
strengths.explanation: The common settings are short, stepwise and singable unaccompanied. Nothing about the music stands between a congregation and the words.

communal.vocalRangeNote: Commonly published in F and G depending on the tune. Short phrases and a narrow compass; among the easier hymns for a mixed room.

range.key: Commonly published in F and G, varying by tune
range.note: No chart was read for this review, so the pitches are not stated. The hymn is sung to several different tunes.

communal.repetitionAssessment: None beyond the opening formula of each verse, which is the device that makes the list audible as a list. Six verses of new material.
communal.assessment: Easy to sing and flexible to programme. Its communal weight is not musical: it has a whole room offer specific things by name, including their money.

strengths.title: Nothing hides behind 'everything'
strengths.explanation: Each verse names one thing. There is no way to sing the hymn and remain unclear about what has been offered, which is exactly the opposite of most surrender songs.

clarity.assessment: Unusually concrete. The hymn's whole method is naming things one at a time, so nothing it asks for is left open to interpretation.

synthesis.summary: A hymn of consecration that refuses to be vague: hands, feet, voice, money and will are each handed over by name, so a congregation hears exactly what it has committed. The will is not softened and the money is not skipped. What it never supplies is the ground — the offering is made without stating what God has done to make it fitting.

scriptureReferences.relevance: The itemised bodily offering the hymn makes — and the mercies it appeals to, which the hymn omits.
Not my will but yours — the surrender the hardest verse asks for.
God and money as rival masters, which is why naming the silver matters.
